name: Persian Green
lede: Persian Green is a strong blue-green; the name is older than the screen color, since an 1906 formula already used it for a mixed pigment of greens.

sections.title: A mixed pigment
sections.body: The Pigment Compendium records two Persian pigments side by side [1]. Persian black was reported by an artist in 1886 to the Russell and Abney committee, and its composition is unknown [1]. Persian green, according to Zerr and Rübencamp in 1906, was mixed from emerald green, imperial green, baryte and pale chrome yellow, in proportions of 75, 45, 20 to 30 and 10 to 20 parts [1]. It is a trade color, not a historic Persian mineral, and the book gives no reason for the name [1].

sections.title: The color name
sections.body: Maerz and Paul recorded Persian Green in 1892, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files it in block 151 [2]. The library's nearest named color is [[jade]], 11.6 units off [2]. For close greens see [[teal]] and [[turquoise]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch is rare in paintings: only 2 of 23,781 match, Matisse's 1906 [[painting:smk-KMSr77|Street in Biskra, Algeria]], where it covers 12 per cent, and Patrick Henry Bruce's *Peinture/Nature Morte* of 1924 [3]. Both date from the 1900s [3]. As photographed: museum photographs of aged, varnished paintings; a color match is not a pigment test.

origin.first_recorded: Maerz & Paul give 1892; Zerr & Rübencamp describe the pigment in 1906

openers: Persian green was once a recipe, not a place: emerald green, imperial green, baryte and chrome yellow.
Matisse's 1906 Biskra street is one of only two paintings in our archive with this blue-green.
